expectations: These come from the Week 6 test (the same detector and tamper code, a different source batch). They are not targets and nothing is tuned to them.

Week 6 test, rule v2: rerender_inconsistent, inplace_edit, page_swap, page_remove and overlay 100/100 tampered each; inplace_edit_consistent 97/100; rerender_consistent 0/100 tampered and 14/100 flagged.
Week 6 test, genuine PDFs: 'tampered' 0/300 on test and 0/300 on shift; 'tampered or suspicious' 7/300 and 5/300, every flag from the anomaly check alone.
So on the blind set: the edit types near 100% tampered, rerender_consistent mostly missed, 'tampered' on genuine PDFs near 0 and 'suspicious' on genuine PDFs near 2%.

Each source is genuine with probability 0.4, so the mix is random and per-type counts are small (on the order of 17 each, fewer for rerender_consistent, which needs a salary): their intervals will be wide.
Anything far from this is reported as it is.
known_limits: Everything is synthetic, and every tampered PDF comes from this project's own tamper code. No outside person edited a PDF.
The seal proves the key was not changed after it was sealed, not that nobody could have read it.
File sizes may differ between genuine and tampered PDFs; the seal hides the mix from the scoring process, not from someone inspecting the files.
data/blind_src/ stays on disk because the rebuild-and-verify check needs it; once the key is published, anyone can rebuild everything anyway.

Genuine PDFs are byte copies of their sources and are not re-saved, because the two re-render types are not written by pypdf, so no re-save step could hide the difference from every tampered copy. The other tampered types are written by pypdf, so file-structure cues may separate them from genuine PDFs; the report gives the numbers without file-history findings. Re-save false alarms are not measured here (Week 6 measured them).
A source that cannot take its drawn type gets another type, so the seven types are not exactly uniform: rerender_consistent, which needs a salary, is probably the rarest.
Per-type counts are small, so most intervals are wide, and a group that is all hits has a zero-width bootstrap interval that is narrower than the real uncertainty.
The bootstrap resamples PDFs. A page_swap donor is another blind source, so a donor's own PDF and a swapped copy are not strictly independent.
A lone anomaly score gives 'suspicious', never 'tampered' (verdict rule v2), and two anomaly features depend indirectly on the Week 3 salary rule (Week 6 limits).

The anomaly threshold and the layout and font baselines came from Week 6's train and dev statements. Before sealing, blind_fresh (a read-only audit that reads the earlier batches under data/ and never the key) found no seed or content shared between the blind sources and any earlier batch; its output was read by hand and is not committed, so this is stated here, not checkable from the repository.

A genuine PDF is a byte copy of a file in data/blind_src/, which stays on disk: hashing a blind PDF against those files identifies the genuine ones before any scoring. Nothing in the pipeline does this, and the seal does not prevent it.
log_run style limit: blind_log does not prevent a second MLflow entry for the same report; the committed report is the record of truth.
metrics: the true mix, counted after the fact (genuine, and each of the seven types)
detection per type as counts, as 'tampered' and as 'tampered or suspicious', with 95% bootstrap intervals over PDFs (1,000 resamples, seed 2026)
the same two counts with every file-history finding removed
false alarms on genuine PDFs, 'tampered' and 'tampered or suspicious', by dialect (default, karan_v1) and overall
precision of a 'tampered' verdict and recall of tampered PDFs (share called 'tampered'), with 95% bootstrap intervals over PDFs
a confusion table of verdict by truth, 'could not check' in its own column
'could not check' and the checks that did not run, per check
a comparison with the Week 6 test numbers
rules: One run only. The sealing command ran once (it never overwrites). The detector, verdict and scoring commands run once each, in the order listed.

The sealing command writes the key, copies it to the backup folder and reads the copy back only to compare hashes; it prints only hashes and counts. Nothing else reads, opens or prints the key before the unseal step, and the detector and the verdict step never read it.

Sealing: a source that cannot take its drawn type (NotApplicable, RebuildError or CopyError) is redrawn to another tamper type from the key's seed, never to genuine; page_swap donors come from the same sub-batch and layout, at most 5 tried. Each RebuildError or CopyError EVENT is recorded in the key and counted (a source that fails twice counts twice, so this counts events, not sources); more than 5 events is a STOP and nothing is written. This is stated for the record: sealing already ran.

The verdict file is committed and pushed BEFORE the unseal step. Scoring refuses a key whose SHA-256 differs from the one recorded here, a verdict file whose SHA-256 differs from the committed one, PDFs whose set hash differs, and a detector fingerprint that differs from Week 6's.
A command that fails with no output: delete its partial output by hand and re-run the identical command once. A second failure is a STOP.
An interrupted detector run may be continued with --resume, which re-checks the detector fingerprint and skips finished chunks; this is not a re-run.

A code change after this file is written needs a new pre-registration (delete this file, re-run the writer, commit and push it) and is disclosed in the report as a post-freeze change. Any run after a first result exists is labelled post-hoc, goes to a file with 'post_hoc' in its name, and never replaces the first result.
A 'tampered' verdict on a genuine PDF is reported with its reasons, never hidden or re-run.
stop_rule: STOP and report, changing nothing: any check above refuses; a second failure of a command that failed with no output.
